old: Yaska's own era, and how much of his work is original versus inherited, remains unclear — earlier, now-lost works on Nirukta likely existed and formed his foundation, though none survive today. Modern scholars, too, are uncertain of his precise date, though most agree he is the Nirukta's author, even if a few Vedic mantras' meanings may not have been entirely clear even to him. Two further complications are worth noting.
new: Many works must have existed as the basis of the Nirukta, but none of them is available now. Though to moderns Yaska's explanations often seem unjustified, without his Nirukta the meaning of many mantras of the Veda would not be known at all. Two points stand out in this matter of the Nirukta.
basis: Kannada p.31 (nirukta-lines): works that were the basis existed, none available; without Yaska many mantras would have no known meaning; two points stand out. English added dating remarks the Kannada does not have

old: Meanings should accord with grammatical rule; irregular or unclear words should be traced to their root; interpreters should favor whichever reading is simplest and most natural; and where two senses seem equally plausible, the one with stronger textual support should be preferred.
new: Where a word is regular in grammar and its meaning bears a direct relation to its root, the derivation should be made directly; where the meaning cannot be found so easily, the derivation should be made on the basis of a similar meaning or similar letters. Everyone who wishes to read and understand the Veda must read the Nirukta; no one can forget the service done by Yaska.
basis: Kannada p.31: vyaakaraNa reetyaa vidhibaddhavaagiddu padada arthakkuu moolapadakkuu neravaada saMbaMdhaviddalli ... samaanavaada artha athavaa samaana akSharagaLa aadhaaradamele niShpatti maaDabeku; nirukta oodabekaagutte; yaaskariMda aagiruva upakaaravannu yaaruu mareyuvahaagilla

old: Jyotisha does not dwell on planetary motion in great technical detail; rather, drawing on the actual observable state of the heavens, it provides the rules used to determine, precisely and impartially, favorable or unfavorable occasions for a person's practical affairs — above all, the correct timing and preparatory rites for yajnas.
new: Jyotisha does not much go into explaining the science of astronomy. These sutras are of no use to those who wish to learn the motions of the planets and from them to fix the good and bad results in a person's life; their aim is to state the planetary motions only so far as is needed to fix the time for performing yajnas and the like and the muhurta at which to begin them.

old: The Lajahoma is the bride's fire-offering of puffed rice. Provision for a widow's remarriage is indicated where circumstances allow. In the Dhruva-darshana, the couple view the fire and then the pole star; in the Arundhati-darshana, the bride views and venerates the star Arundhati — signifying that, following the example of the sage Vasishtha's devoted wife Arundhati, she should conduct herself as a virtuous wife who raises worthy children and manages the household well.
new: Parinaya is the couple's walking round the fire together three times. Aupasana is to be performed by the couple morning and evening for life, the fire established at the marriage being kept at all times for the Aupasana; hence the fire is also called Grihapati. The viewing of the pole star and of Arundhati signifies that the couple should live together lovingly and inseparably, or that, as Arundhati, wife of the sage Vasishtha, was devoted to her husband, the bride should be a devoted wife, serve her husband, bear ten sons and live happily.
